facts.fact: The swim bladder is a gas-filled sac that keeps a fish neutrally buoyant. Without it the fish would sink, because its body is denser than water.
Cyprinids such as goldfish, koi, barbs and rasboras have a two-chambered swim bladder joined by a narrow duct. Most other fish have one chamber.
Swim bladder disorder is a sign with many possible causes, not one disease, so there is no single treatment.
Goldfish are physostomous: a duct links the oesophagus to the swim bladder. Sources link this to how diet and air-gulping can affect buoyancy.
Japanese researchers call the capsizing syndrome of goldfish 'tenpuku disease'. Many cases have no identified cause.
The condition may be temporary or permanent.
Typical signs are floating at the surface or sinking to the bottom, often starting suddenly. The fish may also swim head-down or tilt to one side.
An over-inflated bladder makes the fish rise and float on its side or upside-down. Skin above the water can dry out, ulcerate or become infected.
An under-inflated, collapsed or ruptured bladder, or one with fluid inside, makes the fish sink. Its belly can then get scraped on the substrate.
Affected goldfish usually stay alert and keep eating. Tankmates are often unaffected.
Usually only one fish in a tank is affected.
Outward signs rarely show the underlying cause.
Look-alikes: some infections, ammonia toxicity, and insecticide or pesticide contamination damage the nervous system and cause uncoordinated swimming that resembles a swim bladder problem.
Nitrate poisoning in goldfish causes disorientation, erratic swimming and a C-shaped body. Goldfish tolerate about 20 ppm nitrate before showing signs.
Nitrite toxicity signs can appear at about 0.75 ppm. The safest level for both ammonia and nitrite is 0 ppm.
If a swollen belly comes with raised scales and the fish stops eating, a bacterial infection is more likely.
A fish lying belly-up is not necessarily dead. If it is still breathing, a swim bladder disorder is likely.
An X-ray by a vet is the most reliable diagnostic test. The gas-filled bladder shows as a dark area, revealing its size, position, collapse or fluid content.
Gas building up in the gut, from a gut infection or digestive problem, can make a fish float.
Diet, feeding behaviour and constipation may contribute, especially in goldfish and other cyprinids. The evidence for this is circumstantial.
Surface feeding and gulping air may let gas build up and make the fish float.
Some experts suspect floating pellets or flakes worsen or trigger the problem in round-bodied fancy goldfish. Water temperature also appears to be linked.
Bacterial infections (for example mycobacteria, linked to fluid build-up), viral infections and some fungus-like infections can affect the swim bladder.
Swim bladder infection is usually part of a larger, whole-body (systemic) infection.
Internal tumours or a nearby diseased organ can compress or displace the swim bladder. Tumours are untreatable and usually fatal.
Genetic or developmental defects and abnormal body shapes make fish more prone. Examples are inbred convict cichlids, blood parrot cichlids and fancy goldfish.
Sudden temperature changes can cause buoyancy problems, for example adding very cold water to a tropical tank.
Physical injury, common in territorial fish such as cichlids, and heavy loads of parasitic worms in the gut are further causes.
Other causes reported by keepers: fatty liver, kidney cysts, egg-bound females, and a damaged or blocked duct between gut and swim bladder.
Very pregnant livebearers such as mollies and guppies, and overweight fish, can also swim abnormally.
Low oxygen is more likely in warm water, in tanks without aeration, or in fish with gill disease, and it impairs swimming.
High nitrogenous waste or a rapid temperature drop (reported in pond fish) have been linked to the problem, but the evidence is mostly anecdotal.
Always test the water (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate) and fix any problems, whether or not they seem to be the cause.
If ammonia or nitrite is high, do frequent partial water changes. In severe cases the page suggests 30% to 50% every 4 hours, plus siphoning waste from the substrate.
If the problem looks like shock, turn the lights off so the fish can rest. Recovery often takes a few hours.
Move the sick fish to a separate tank with clean, well-aerated water.
For a fish lying on the bottom, lower the water to about half. For a floating fish, reduce the filter current and add floating plants to support it.
Keep the water only a few inches above the fish so it is not left exposed to air.
For floating goldfish or other cyprinids, try a few days without food or feed crushed cooked peas to clear the gut. The source calls this harmless and worth trying.
Keepers' protocol: fast for 2–3 days, then feed a cooked, peeled, mashed pea.
If the belly is swollen and the fish refuses food, fast for 1–2 days, then resume feeding.
If the water is below 22°C, raise the temperature a little.
If it does not improve, keepers raise the temperature to 78–80°F and add salt at 8 teaspoons per 5 gallons.

In a hospital tank filled with water from the main tank, the heater can be set up to 9°F above the main tank. Some species cannot take warm water or the lower oxygen that comes with it, so keep within the species' tolerance.
Peas suit omnivorous fish only and should not be fed to bettas. For bettas, use live foods with a chitin shell instead, such as water bugs, daphnia (bo bo) or artemia.
If fasting and peas fail, see a vet for X-rays and possibly antibiotics if a bacterial infection is suspected.
For bacterial infection: treat in a separate tank, because the drugs can harm the main tank's beneficial bacteria. KanaPlex or Maracyn 2 are used at the maker's dose.
Antibiotics work better mixed into food than added to the water. Adding them straight to the water has little effect.
Home-made medicated food: 5 g gelatin, 60 g hot water, 30 g dry food and about 0.5 g antibiotic. Feed at least 2 times a day for 10 days, keep it in the fridge and use it for 10 days only.
Also bathe the fish at least once a day in methylene blue and salt to prevent outside infections.
Standard antibiotics may work for bacterial swim bladder infection, but results are uncertain. Small fish often need euthanasia, while larger fish can recover.
Viral infections are virtually impossible to treat.
Treat parasitic gut worms with an antihelminthic (dewormer) medication.
A vet can vent excess gas from an over-inflated bladder with a needle, but the effect is often only temporary.
Surgical weights or external floats can correct buoyancy, but they do not treat the cause.

In goldfish, medical and surgical treatments often give poor results. Vets tested a Floy anchor tag with a small cork float placed in the back muscle under anaesthesia. The first fabric tag was expelled within five days.
Salt and antibiotics can harm the tank's beneficial bacteria, so watch water quality closely, especially when the water level is lowered.
Where a body part sticks out of the water, keepers apply a thin layer of Vaseline.
Many cases do not improve. Euthanasia may be the kindest option, and deformed fry cannot be treated.

1) Test the water and fix ammonia, nitrite or nitrate problems. 2) Move the fish to a hospital tank. 3) Fast for 2–3 days, then feed peas (omnivores only). 4) Raise the temperature gently. 5) If there is no improvement after a few days, consider antibiotics or a vet.
Feed sinking food, or soak pellets until they sink, so fish swallow less air. Keep goldfish water above about 70°F.
Keep nitrate below 20 ppm.
Feed only what the fish eat in about 3 minutes, vary the diet (dry, live foods and greens) and skip feeding one day a week.
Change 10–15% of the water each week and siphon the substrate about every 2 weeks. Avoid sudden temperature changes and overcrowding.
Give fancy fish a fibre-rich diet, quarantine new fish to prevent parasitic worms, avoid aggressive tankmates and breed carefully.
Feed small meals once or twice a day, only as much as the fish eat in 3 to 5 minutes. Cycle the tank and keep good biological filtration.
Common mistakes: overfeeding or low-quality food, changing too much water at once, letting the temperature swing quickly, feeding peas to bettas, and putting antibiotics in the main tank.
Weights or floats only fix buoyancy and leave the cause untreated.

In Vietnam, one keeper uses metronidazole and prefers Megyna (metronidazole plus chloramphenicol) at 1 tablet per 10 litres in purified water. US products such as Medigold and Metromed are not available.
Above 76°F (≈24°C), increase aeration. This matters in Vietnam's warm climate, where warm water holds less oxygen.

Vietnamese keepers try roasted sesame seeds as a substitute for peas, which they find harder to get. Soaked seeds go mouldy within about a day, so remove leftovers at once. This is personal experience, not tested.
Vietnamese sources disagree on peas for bettas. Aquasetup says peas can make bettas worse, while some other Vietnamese sites recommend them.
Myth: every fish that floats or swims erratically has a swim bladder problem. Practical Fishkeeping says infections, toxins and gut gas cause the same signs.
Myth: fasting or peas are a proven cure. Practical Fishkeeping says they are widely claimed and worth trying, but not guaranteed.
If the fish does not respond after several weeks of treatment, the condition is likely permanent.
